prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 800 words of John Snow's investigation of the 1854 cholera outbreak around Broad Street in London. The reader is a general reader with no medical background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
In the summer of 1854 cholera returned to London. The disease causes violent diarrhoea and vomiting, and in its worst cases the body loses so much water that a person can die within a day or two. It had first reached Britain in 1831 and had come back several times since, killing tens of thousands. Most doctors held that it was carried in foul air, which they called miasma and believed rose from rotting waste and damp ground. John Snow, a physician living in Soho, did not accept that explanation.

Snow was forty-one. He was born in York, the son of a labourer, and had been apprenticed to a surgeon before moving to London. By 1854 he was best known as a specialist in anaesthetics, and he had given chloroform to Queen Victoria at the birth of her son in 1853. In 1849 he had published a short pamphlet arguing that cholera was caused by something swallowed, and that it passed from the bowels of the sick into water that other people later drank. He had little direct evidence for this, and few of his colleagues were persuaded.

The outbreak that gave him his evidence began in the last days of August in the streets around Broad Street, which is now called Broadwick Street. Snow lived a short walk away in Sackville Street. In the three days after 31 August, 127 people in the area died, and many residents left their homes. By the time the outbreak ended, about 616 people had died.

Snow obtained the list of cholera deaths from the Registrar General and went from house to house asking where each household got its drinking water. He found that most of the dead lived close to the public pump in Broad Street. Of 83 deaths he had checked by 6 September, 73 were in houses nearer to that pump than to any other. Of the remaining ten, he was told that the families of five had always sent to the Broad Street pump anyway, and three of the dead were children who went to school near it.

The cases that did not fit the pattern mattered as much to him. The workhouse in Poland Street held 535 people and had only five deaths. It had its own well and did not use the Broad Street pump. A brewery in the same street employed about seventy men, and none of them died. The brewery also had its own well, and the men were given malt liquor to drink. Snow also learned of a widow in Hampstead, far from Soho, who had died of cholera on 2 September. She had once lived in Broad Street, and she liked the taste of its water so much that a cart brought a bottle of it to her each day. A niece who drank from the same supply also died. Few other people in Hampstead fell ill at that time.

Snow could not show what was in the water. He looked at a sample under a microscope and saw nothing that proved his case. On 7 September he took his findings to the Board of Guardians of St James's parish, which was responsible for the district. The board was not convinced, but it agreed to act, and the next day the handle was taken off the pump so that nobody could draw water from it.

The number of new cases had already been falling before that day, partly because so many people had left. Snow said this himself, and later writers have disagreed about how much the removal of the handle changed the course of the outbreak. That is a matter of judgement, and the figures do not settle it.

A local curate, Henry Whitehead, helped to complete the account. He knew the neighbourhood and its people well, and at first he thought Snow was wrong. He carried out his own inquiries and traced the first case to a baby girl at 40 Broad Street, who had fallen ill on 28 August and died on 2 September. Her mother had washed the child's soiled nappies and poured the water into a cesspool in the cellar. The cesspool was only about three feet from the well that fed the pump, and its brick lining was found to be decayed. Whitehead came to agree with Snow.

Official bodies took longer to do so. The General Board of Health reviewed the outbreak in 1855 and kept to the view that bad air was the cause. Snow published a second edition of his pamphlet that year, with a map that marked each death with a bar at the address where it happened, so that the crowding of bars around the Broad Street pump could be seen at a glance. He died in 1858 at the age of forty-five, still without a general acceptance of his theory.

The organism that causes cholera was first seen in Florence in 1854 by Filippo Pacini, whose work went unnoticed, and was identified again by Robert Koch in 1883. From 1859 London began building a large system of sewers, which carried waste away from the river and from the wells. Snow's method of recording where cases occurred, and then looking for what they had in common, became a standard way of studying disease.
